readerTitle: One angry email: how far should it change your mind?
caseNote: 가상 사례 (보험사 내부 팀의 업무 도구 출시, 식료품 체인의 과자 구매 담당) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 증거는 '맞다/틀리다'로 판정하는 것이 아니다. '내가 맞을 때와 틀릴 때 이 증거가 각각 얼마나 자주 나오는가'를 비교해, 그 차이만큼만 확신을 움직인다.
misconception: 새 증거가 나오면 생각을 통째로 바꾸거나(한 건의 불만에 롤백), 반대로 기존 믿음을 지키려고 무시해야 한다. 크게 들리는 증거일수록 강한 증거다.

sources.text: Bayes, T. (1763). An Essay towards solving a Problem in the Doctrine of Chances. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society.

factChecks.note: 계산 확인: 출시 100건 중 문제 있음 20건, 문제 없음 80건. 문제 없는 출시의 50%(40건), 문제 있는 출시의 90%(18건)가 첫 주에 불만 메일을 받음. 메일이 온 58건 중 문제 있는 출시 18건 → 18 ÷ 58 = 31.0%. 사전 확률 20% → 사후 확률 약 31%.
Thomas Bayes는 18세기 영국의 장로교 목사이며, 관련 논문은 사후인 1763년 Richard Price를 통해 발표되었습니다. 게시 전 표현("18th-century English minister")을 다시 확인하세요.
'사람들은 자신이 자랑스러워하는 계획에 대해 경고를 덜 반영하는 경향이 있다'는 문장은 확증 편향에 관한 일반적 서술로, 특정 연구 수치를 인용하지 않았습니다. 수치를 붙이지 않도록 유지하세요.
영업 담당자 사례, 새 과자 브랜드 대부분이 1년을 못 간다는 설정은 가상 설정입니다. 실제 신제품 실패율 통계로 바꾸려면 1차 출처가 필요합니다.

cards.title: One angry email: how far should it change your mind?
body: Tuesday, 9:12 a.m. Your team rolled out a new claims tool to 400 colleagues last week. A director forwards one email: "This tool is a mess. Nobody can find anything."
Your stomach drops. But one email is a piece of evidence, not a verdict. The real question is how far it should move you.

image.label: A manager staring at one forwarded email on a laptop
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 사무실 책상에서 노트북 화면에 빨간 느낌표가 달린 이메일 한 통이 떠 있고, 관리자가 커피잔을 든 채 굳어 있음. 화면 옆에 작은 다이얼(확신 게이지)이 살짝 흔들리는 모습. 실제 회사 로고나 메일 서비스 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: The first complaint lands.
body: You lead a small team at a large insurance company. Testing went well before launch, and you were fairly sure the new tool works. Then the angry email arrives.

options.text: Pause the rollout and switch everyone back to the old tool
options.feedback: You guard against a real problem, but you let one voice outweigh all your testing. Rollbacks cost time and trust too.

options.text: Ignore it. One email proves nothing
options.feedback: You keep momentum, but you throw away a real signal. If the tool is broken, this is exactly how you'd hear first.

options.text: Lower your confidence a little, then check how many complaints the old tool got in a normal week
options.feedback: You treat the email as evidence, then ask how surprising it really is. That tells you how far to move.

cards.title: Run the launch 100 times.
body: Say 20 of every 100 launches like yours hide a real problem. Some people complain about any change, so half the fine launches still get an angry email in week one. Nearly all broken ones do: 18 of 20.
That's 58 launches with an email, and 18 are broken. The chance of a real problem rises from 20% to about **31%**. Worth a look. Not a reason to panic.

groups.label: Chance the tool has a real problem

cards.title: Updating your beliefs
body: **Updating your beliefs** means treating confidence as a dial, not a switch. You start with your best guess, then turn it up or down each time new evidence arrives.
How far you turn it depends on one question: *how much more likely is this evidence if I'm right than if I'm wrong?* The math behind it is named after Thomas Bayes, an 18th-century English minister.

image.label: A confidence dial moving from 20% to 31%
image.brief: 아날로그 다이얼 인포그래픽. 바늘이 "20%"에서 "31%"로 조금 이동하고, 옆에 "New evidence" 라벨이 붙은 작은 이메일 아이콘. 스위치(ON/OFF)에 X 표시를 해서 '스위치가 아니라 다이얼'임을 대비.

cards.title: Ask the two-sided question.
body: Every new piece of evidence gets the same three steps:
list: **Start with a number:** how likely did this seem before?
**Compare two worlds:** how often would you see this evidence if you're right, and how often if you're wrong?
**Move in proportion:** a big gap moves you a lot. No gap moves you not at all.
cards.callout: Evidence that shows up equally in both worlds isn't really evidence.
cards.softwareNote: Monitoring alerts work the same way. An alert that fires on half of healthy days tells you little. One that fires only when something is truly broken deserves an instant response.

cards.title: Loud is not the same as strong.
body: The email felt huge because a director forwarded it. But rank changes how loud evidence is, not how strong it is. It's still one complaint.
Strong evidence looks different: support tickets tripling, or colleagues who never complain all saying the same thing. Those are rare when things are fine and common when they're not.
Evidence also adds up. Several weak, unrelated signals pointing the same way can move you as far as one strong one.

cards.title: You can update too little or too much.
body: Move too little, and you explain away every warning. People often do this with plans they're proud of. Move too much, and you swing with every email.
Check that signals are truly separate. Ten complaints from one office that sat through the same bad training count closer to one.
And updates are only as good as the starting guess. If that number was wishful, every update inherits the wish.

image.label: Two dials: one stuck, one spinning wildly
image.brief: 다이얼 두 개 나란히. 왼쪽은 자물쇠가 걸려 바늘이 꼼짝 않음("Too little"), 오른쪽은 바늘이 회오리처럼 빙빙 돎("Too much"). 가운데에 바늘이 적당히 움직이는 작은 다이얼("Just enough").

cards.title: Now it's a grocery chain.
body: You buy snacks for 30 grocery stores. Most new snack brands you've stocked don't last a year on the shelf.
A supplier's sales rep visits and says a new chip brand is "flying off shelves" at other chains. What's your move?

options.text: Order it for all 30 stores. The rep sees the whole market
options.feedback: Fast if the rep is right. But reps say this about almost every product, so the claim is about as likely if the chips are a flop.

options.text: Ask for sell-through data from other chains, then test it in a few stores
options.feedback: Real sales numbers are much rarer for a flop than for a hit, so they can actually move you. A small test adds your own evidence cheaply.

options.text: Pass. Most new snacks fail anyway
options.feedback: Your starting point is sound, but you refuse to look at any evidence. A real hit would slip right past you.

cards.title: Ask how surprising the evidence is, then move that far.
body: Confidence is a dial. Each new fact should turn it by an amount set by how much more likely that fact is if you're right than if you're wrong.
**Try it today:** pick one belief about your business, like "our new price is working." Write your confidence as a percentage. When news arrives, ask the two-sided question before you react.
